stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Groundwater levels beneath the High Plains have been falling for decades, but not at the same rate everywhere. After mapping forty years of well records, ______ that the steepest declines cluster where irrigation wells sit less than a kilometer apart, a pattern suggesting that neighboring pumps draw down the same pocket of water faster than rainfall can refill it.
explanation: There is no article ('the' or 'a') before 'hydrologist,' so 'hydrologist Tomás Reyna' works as one label for the subject, and the name can't be fenced off. The subject 'hydrologist Tomás Reyna' then leads straight into its verb 'found,' and nothing should separate a subject from its verb. So you use no punctuation at all.

A.why: You treated the name as a removable appositive, as in 'my friend, Ana, said.' With no article before 'hydrologist,' the name is essential: if you remove it, you're left with 'hydrologist found,' which doesn't work. So the pair of commas is wrong.

C.why: You got the title and name right but put a comma after the name. That comma splits the subject 'hydrologist Tomás Reyna' from its verb 'found,' and nothing should come between them.

D.why: A colon has to follow a complete sentence. 'After mapping forty years of well records, hydrologist' isn't one, so the colon has nothing to introduce.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most self-healing polymers repair cracks only when they are heated, which limits their usefulness on bridges, ship hulls, and other surfaces exposed to cold air. A coating developed by ______ scratches at room temperature. Its surface is laced with microscopic capsules of liquid resin that burst when scraped, filling the gap and hardening within a few hours.
explanation: 'Materials scientist' has no article in front of it, so 'materials scientist Adaeze Okafor' is a single label and takes no internal punctuation. Now cross out 'developed by materials scientist Adaeze Okafor.' What's left is 'A coating seals scratches.' The verb 'seals' belongs to 'coating,' and no mark should come between that subject and its verb.

B.why: You put a comma between the title and the name, as if the name were an optional add-on. Without an article, the title and name form one label, so the comma breaks it apart. That comma also has no partner to close it.

C.why: The comma after the name sits between the subject 'A coating developed by…' and its verb 'seals.' One comma can't separate a subject from its verb, no matter how long the subject is.

D.why: A pair of dashes works like a pair of commas: it marks something you could remove. Here the name can't be removed, because 'developed by materials scientist seals' falls apart. So you shouldn't set it off with dashes.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Oakhaven's pocket parks—small plazas built on unused traffic islands, a strategy first proposed by ______ draw more weekday visitors than the city's largest park. City surveys suggest the reason is distance: nearly every resident now lives within a five-minute walk of one, while the large park lies at the edge of town.
explanation: This question has two steps. First, 'urban planner' has no article in front of it, so 'urban planner Lena Marchetti' takes no punctuation inside. Second, a dash after 'parks' opened an interruption much earlier, and it ends with the name. So it must close with a matching dash. Cross out the interruption and you get 'Oakhaven's pocket parks now draw more weekday visitors,' a complete sentence.

A.why: You noticed the interruption had to close but used a comma to close it. It opened with a dash, and the marks around an interruption have to match. A dash can't be paired with a comma.

B.why: The closing dash is right, but you added an appositive comma between the title and the name. With no article in front, 'urban planner Lena Marchetti' is one label and can't be split.

C.why: You correctly left the title and name unpunctuated but forgot the dash that opened after 'parks.' Without a closing dash, the interruption runs into the main verb, and the sentence no longer holds together.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Rowers are often told that a long, static stretch before a race prevents injury and adds power. Australian ______ the claim with forty collegiate athletes, comparing static stretching with a brief dynamic warm-up of leg swings and light strokes. The dynamic group produced more force over the first five hundred meters, and injury rates for the two groups were nearly identical.
explanation: 'Australian sports scientist' has a nationality in front of it but no article ('the' or 'a'). So 'Australian sports scientist Priya Natarajan' works as one label and is the subject of the sentence. It leads straight into the verb 'tested' with no punctuation anywhere.

A.why: You used the appositive habit of putting a comma before the name. Without an article, the name is part of the label, so nothing goes between 'sports scientist' and 'Priya Natarajan.'

B.why: A single dash works like a colon, so it needs a complete sentence before it. 'Australian sports scientist' isn't a sentence. The dash also cuts the subject apart.

D.why: The title and name are right, but the comma after 'Natarajan' separates the subject from its verb 'tested.' A subject and its verb shouldn't be split by a single comma.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Cover crops such as cereal rye can return nitrogen to depleted fields, yet farmers who plant them often report uneven results. Drawing on six seasons of plot trials, Iowa ______ identified the deciding factor: when the rye is killed off. Fields where it was terminated two weeks before planting consistently yielded more corn than fields where it was left growing until planting day.
explanation: 'Iowa agronomist' has no article in front of it, so 'Iowa agronomist Malik Osei' is a single label that serves as the subject. It runs straight into the verb 'has identified' with no punctuation. The colon belongs later in the sentence, after the complete clause that promises 'the deciding factor,' and not inside the subject.

A.why: You treated the name as a removable appositive. Take it out and you get 'Iowa agronomist has identified,' which needs an article to work. That shows the name is essential, so it can't be fenced off with commas.

B.why: The comma after 'Osei' comes between the subject and its verb 'has identified.' A single comma there splits the sentence's core in two.

C.why: You may have spotted that the sentence uses a colon and put one too early. A colon needs a complete sentence before it, and 'Drawing on six seasons of plot trials, Iowa agronomist' isn't one.
